interpretations.rationale: Source account (no retained execution). The checked-in ReadOnlySafe flow stores a peer-supplied Context byte string as a read-position ack without any equality check against the positions the leader emitted (read_only.go recvAck/AckedIndex), then derives a quorum position from those stored values and slices unconfirmedReads by it (read_only.go maybeAdvance via quorum.CommittedIndex). A focused local probe on the unexported readOnly, run only as native feedback and not retained as a receipt, reproduced two mechanical consequences when acks carry a value the leader never emitted: (a) three voters with two over-large ack values produced a panic 'slice bounds out of range [:1099511627776] with capacity 1', because newConfirmedReads-confirmedReads exceeded len(unconfirmedReads); (b) with two admitted reads, a single over-large ack combined with the leader's own self-ack reached a 2-of-3 quorum position and confirmed the second read even though that voter had received no heartbeat carrying it, i.e. the response that justifies the read index was not actually observed by a quorum. Both consequences require a Context value outside the set heartbeatCtx emits. Within the crash-fault model the checked-in producers only echo the leader's context (handleHeartbeat copies m.Context; lower-term responses are dropped by raft.Step), so the fact @K_read_pos holds for faithful participants and I have not established an in-model trigger; the v3.6.0 contrast (recvAck keyed acks by exact pending request context and ignored unknown contexts) shows the validation is a deliberate-or-incidental regression of the rewrite rather than a pre-existing property, but a historical comparison is not by itself evidence about reachability here. Counterevidence/limits: (1) the premise is a Context the leader never issued, which is a fault-model violation unless a legal producer exists - this is exactly the open gap; (2) the probe drove readOnly directly, supplying read messages, so it demonstrates the predicate mechanically and not a network path; (3) no retained receipt was produced, so no execution indices are cited. Related in-model pressure noted but not promoted to a claim: addRequest no longer deduplicates by request context, so the same documented retry pattern ('user's job to ensure read index retries') appends one unconfirmed entry and broadcasts one heartbeat per retry for as long as the leader cannot reach quorum confirmation. Because applicability hinges on the missing producer rather than on reproducing the symptom, the defect judgment stays unresolved and the gap above records what would settle it.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account, no retained execution (native feedback only when it could change the reading). Predicate under test: does a postponed MsgReadIndex ever get completed with a read index below its admission-time committed index after surviving an authority transition? Admission: stepLeader queues the message whenever committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is false (:1355-1372); the message carries no index and no term, so nothing about admission is cached. Survival: raft.reset (:781-812) reassigns readOnly and clears votes, progress, pendingConfIndex and uncommittedSize but never touches pendingReadIndexMessages, so the slice persists across step-down, re-election and removal; the deferral is therefore a real queued duty that outlives the leadership under which it was accepted. Completion: releasePendingReadIndexMessages is reached only from the leader's MsgAppResp path where maybeCommit() returned true (:1546-1556) and re-checks committedEntryInCurrentTerm() before acting, so release happens under current leadership in the current term; the index passed to sendMsgReadIndexResponse is r.raftLog.committed read at that moment, not a value captured earlier. Monotonicity: commitTo only assigns when l.committed < tocommit (log.go :322-330); log restore is reached only after the guard that the snapshot index exceeds the current committed (log.go :463-470); loadState panics unless state.commit is >= committed and <= lastIndex (raft.go :2037-2047); maybeAppend commits min(upstream commit, lastnewi). Hence committed never decreases across the serialized event sequence, release is strictly later than admission, and the completed index is >= the admission-time index. The suspicion of a stale read index from a surviving queue is therefore defeated in-model. Retained and still relevant: (a) the queue is deliberately not cleared, so a request queued under a term whose successor leadership never commits in term leaves the duty pending until the client's documented retry; (b) the release path is the only completion producer, so if the node never leads again the duty is never completed by this node - this matches the documented contract that ReadIndex requests can be lost and are the caller's retry responsibility, so it is a contract property rather than a defect; (c) this is a source-only conclusion, so a later retained execution would be needed to turn it into an observation. Independent uncertainty not promoted to a claim: because release recomputes the index, a request postponed under an earlier term can be answered with an index above what it needed, which is safe for linearizability but means the answered index does not identify the request's original position.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: under the library's stated contract, a follower placed in StateSnapshot has an enabled repair. Source account only. Evidence for the predicate: the library provides one peer-driven repair (a MsgAppResp that strictly advances pr.Match while pr.Match+1 >= firstIndex triggers BecomeProbe/BecomeReplicate) and one explicitly documented application-driven repair (ReportSnapshot, delivered as MsgSnapStatus, which is accepted only while pr.State == StateSnapshot and then clears PendingSnapshot on failure and becomes a probe). The Progress comment at tracker/progress.go :64-84 states this design intent, including that the application must report snapshot failure so the leader resumes probing, and node.go's ReportSnapshot documentation makes that an explicit application duty. I checked for a self-repair path: heartbeats to a paused follower produce MsgHeartbeatResp, but the heartbeat handler's sendAppend is a no-op because IsPaused is true in StateSnapshot, and no timer exits the state; so the library alone does not repair a lost MsgAppResp. That is a responsibility boundary rather than a defect: the local duty (resume replication once either event arrives) is implemented and reachable, and the external event is owed by the application under the documented contract. Boundaries and counterevidence: (a) the trace is source-only with no retained receipt; (b) if an application enabled snapshots but never called ReportSnapshot, a follower whose snapshot response was lost would stay paused, which is a contract violation by the caller, not a target defect; (c) handleSnapshot's ignored-snapshot branch replies with r.raftLog.committed, whose value can be at or below pr.Match, in which case MaybeUpdate is false and that particular MsgAppResp does not repair - the report path remains the required mechanism, consistent with the Progress comment. No defect claim is made; the value here is the recorded responsibility boundary and the exact exit conditions.

interpretations.rationale: The gap is answered (resolved=true) and the scoped defect is now asserted rather than left unresolved. Conditions of the defect, all of them permitted: the node is a legitimate leader of a three-voter configuration; CheckQuorum is false, which is the library default and which ReadOnlySafe does not require to change; the leader cannot obtain quorum acknowledgements, so committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is false and every read request takes the pending path; the caller follows the documented contract and retries ReadIndex with the same RequestCtx. Under those conditions the library accumulates one pending read request per retry with no collapsing and no bound, and retains them even after the node is deposed, so the state grows with caller retries and is never reclaimed by the library. Evidence: sources give the per-request, context-blind admission and the untouched queue in raft.reset; a focused probe against the real FSM (native feedback in this session, repeated by the fixed experiment submitted with this record) showed a real leader at term 1 with committed=0/lastIndex=1, CheckQuorum=false and the default ReadOnlySafe option, then 64 same-context retries with no quorum acknowledgement yielding pending=64 and unconfirmed=0 while still StateLeader, and pending_after=64 with unconfirmed_after=0 after a higher-term heartbeat deposed it to StateFollower. The experiment's two comparisons assert exactly those two counts against the recorded admission; the controller owns that receipt and its parsed indices, so none are cited here yet. Why this is a defect rather than correct behaviour: not answering a read without quorum is correct and is not the complaint - the complaint is that the library accepts and retains an unbounded number of these requests and their retained message pointers, so the memory footprint is driven by caller retries rather than by any decision the library makes, and no enabled mechanism reduces it (the release path requires this node to lead again in a term where it commits, and only then does it drain the whole queue at once, each entry additionally triggering an admission and heartbeat broadcast through sendMsgReadIndexResponse). Counterevidence and limits I considered and did not let defeat the claim: (a) a leader without quorum cannot answer reads, so nonprogress itself is not the defect - I scope the claim to accumulation and retention; (b) a caller that retries without bound is the party repeatedly recreating the obligation, but the contract states no bound and gives it no way to observe that its request is still queued, so this is a missing library-side bound rather than a calling restriction; (c) with a healthy quorum each retry is confirmed on the next heartbeat response, so this is not a steady-state cost; (d) the removal of context-keyed handling is the v3.7.0 stale-index fix and I am not contesting that fix, only the absence of a size limit around it. interpretations.rationale: Source account plus one focused probe (native feedback only; no retained receipt). Sources establish the mechanism: node.run's lead-change branch re-assigns propc on any transition to a non-None leader, while the removal branch sets it to nil only at the moment the removal is applied and is accompanied by an in-tree comment admitting the logic is unsound; stepFollower's MsgProp case forwards to r.lead unconditionally; stepLeader's MsgProp case checks only the leader's own membership. The probe drove the real FSM directly: with voters {1,2,3}, a leader that applied a ConfChange removing node 3 reported voters [1 2] with Progress[3] deleted, and yet stepping a MsgProp with From=3 returned nil and appended one entry (lastIndex 1 to 2); a separate instance for node 3, made a follower of node 2 and then made to apply its own removal, still forwarded a local MsgProp to node 2. So the raft-level half of the hypothesis is confirmed, and the facade half follows from the source reading. Why this stays unresolved rather than asserted: the decisive question is ownership of sender eligibility. Raft's contract is about replication and commit quorums; a proposal is data to be replicated, and the library documents that proposals can be lost and that the caller must retry, but it does not document that raft authorizes the proposer. If authorization belongs to the application, then the leader appending a non-member's entry is not a defect - the application chose to forward it - and node.go's comment is only about a local convenience; if the intent really is to block proposals from a removed node, then the leader-change re-enablement is a defect because it silently revives a channel the code deliberately closed. I did not let the probe settle that, and I did not weaken the question by treating the comment as proof of the intended contract. Counterevidence and limits: (a) RawNode users bypass the facade entirely and can step any MsgProp, which supports the caller-owns-authorization reading; (b) DisableProposalForwarding exists precisely so an operator can stop members from forwarding, implying forwarding by members is normal and by non-members is a configuration concern; (c) the removal branch checks okBefore so a node that never knew it was a member is not blocked; (d) my probe modified no production logic and used only public/package-internal entry points. interpretations.rationale: Source account (no retained execution). The checked-in ReadOnlySafe flow stores a peer-supplied Context byte string as a read-position ack without any equality check against the positions the leader emitted (read_only.go recvAck/AckedIndex), then derives a quorum position from those stored values and slices unconfirmedReads by it (read_only.go maybeAdvance via quorum.CommittedIndex). A focused local probe on the unexported readOnly, run only as native feedback and not retained as a receipt, reproduced two mechanical consequences when acks carry a value the leader never emitted: (a) three voters with two over-large ack values produced a panic 'slice bounds out of range [:1099511627776] with capacity 1', because newConfirmedReads-confirmedReads exceeded len(unconfirmedReads); (b) with two admitted reads, a single over-large ack combined with the leader's own self-ack reached a 2-of-3 quorum position and confirmed the second read even though that voter had received no heartbeat carrying it, i.e. the response that justifies the read index was not actually observed by a quorum. Both consequences require a Context value outside the set heartbeatCtx emits. Within the crash-fault model the checked-in producers only echo the leader's context (handleHeartbeat copies m.Context; lower-term responses are dropped by raft.Step), so the fact @K_read_pos holds for faithful participants and I have not established an in-model trigger; the v3.6.0 contrast (recvAck keyed acks by exact pending request context and ignored unknown contexts) shows the validation is a deliberate-or-incidental regression of the rewrite rather than a pre-existing property, but a historical comparison is not by itself evidence about reachability here. interpretations.rationale: Source-only account, no retained execution (native feedback only when it could change the reading). Predicate under test: does a postponed MsgReadIndex ever get completed with a read index below its admission-time committed index after surviving an authority transition? Admission: stepLeader queues the message whenever committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is false (:1355-1372); the message carries no index and no term, so nothing about admission is cached. Survival: raft.reset (:781-812) reassigns readOnly and clears votes, progress, pendingConfIndex and uncommittedSize but never touches pendingReadIndexMessages, so the slice persists across step-down, re-election and removal; the deferral is therefore a real queued duty that outlives the leadership under which it was accepted. Completion: releasePendingReadIndexMessages is reached only from the leader's MsgAppResp path where maybeCommit() returned true (:1546-1556) and re-checks committedEntryInCurrentTerm() before acting, so release happens under current leadership in the current term; the index passed to sendMsgReadIndexResponse is r.raftLog.committed read at that moment, not a value captured earlier. Monotonicity: commitTo only assigns when l.committed < tocommit (log.go :322-330); log restore is reached only after the guard that the snapshot index exceeds the current committed (log.go :463-470); loadState panics unless state.commit is >= committed and <= lastIndex (raft.go :2037-2047); maybeAppend commits min(upstream commit, lastnewi). Hence committed never decreases across the serialized event sequence, release is strictly later than admission, and the completed index is >= the admission-time index. The suspicion of a stale read index from a surviving queue is therefore defeated in-model. Retained and still relevant: (a) the queue is deliberately not cleared, so a request queued under a term whose successor leadership never commits in term leaves the duty pending until the client's documented retry; (b) the release path is the only completion producer, so if the node never leads again the duty is never completed by this node - this matches the documented contract that ReadIndex requests can be lost and are the caller's retry responsibility, so it is a contract property rather than a defect; (c) this is a source-only conclusion, so a later retained execution would be needed to turn it into an observation. Independent uncertainty not promoted to a claim: because release recomputes the index, a request postponed under an earlier term can be answered with an index above what it needed, which is safe for linearizability but means the answered index does not identify the request's original position.

Sources establish the mechanism: node.run's lead-change branch re-assigns propc on any transition to a non-None leader, while the removal branch sets it to nil only at the moment the removal is applied and is accompanied by an in-tree comment admitting the logic is unsound; stepFollower's MsgProp case forwards to r.lead unconditionally; stepLeader's MsgProp case checks only the leader's own membership. The probe drove the real FSM directly: with voters {1,2,3}, a leader that applied a ConfChange removing node 3 reported voters [1 2] with Progress[3] deleted, and yet stepping a MsgProp with From=3 returned nil and appended one entry (lastIndex 1 to 2); a separate instance for node 3, made a follower of node 2 and then made to apply its own removal, still forwarded a local MsgProp to node 2. So the raft-level half of the hypothesis is confirmed, and the facade half follows from the source reading. Why this stays unresolved rather than asserted: the decisive question is ownership of sender eligibility. Raft's contract is about replication and commit quorums; a proposal is data to be replicated, and the library documents that proposals can be lost and that the caller must retry, but it does not document that raft authorizes the proposer. If authorization belongs to the application, then the leader appending a non-member's entry is not a defect - the application chose to forward it - and node.go's comment is only about a local convenience; if the intent really is to block proposals from a removed node, then the leader-change re-enablement is a defect because it silently revives a channel the code deliberately closed. I did not let the probe settle that, and I did not weaken the question by treating the comment as proof of the intended contract. Counterevidence and limits: (a) RawNode users bypass the facade entirely and can step any MsgProp, which supports the caller-owns-authorization reading; (b) DisableProposalForwarding exists precisely so an operator can stop members from forwarding, implying forwarding by members is normal and by non-members is a configuration concern; (c) the removal branch checks okBefore so a node that never knew it was a member is not blocked; (d) my probe modified no production logic and used only public/package-internal entry points. The gap above records what would settle it, and the behaviour is recorded as a fact without a defect judgment.

interpretations.rationale: Resolution of the earlier conditional account. What changed: I stopped treating node.go's comment as the contract and read what the library actually documents. doc.go:305-316 describes MsgProp as a redirection mechanism - the leader appends entries to its log and broadcasts them, a candidate drops them, and a follower stores them with the sender's ID for forwarding - with no eligibility condition anywhere, and no statement in doc.go, node.go or README assigns proposer authorization to the library. That is decisive for the gap, because the question was which of the two readings the library promises: the documented behaviour is exactly what the probe measured, so the leader accepting a proposal whose sender is no longer in the configuration is the contract working as written, not a defect, and the whole suspicion is refuted. The behaviour gathered earlier remains valid and is retained as facts: the facade re-enables the proposal channel on any observed leader change regardless of membership (node.go:366-380), the removal branch that nils the channel is accompanied by a comment calling the logic unsound (node.go:400-432), stepFollower forwards MsgProp to r.lead without a membership test (raft.go:1720-1730), and stepping a MsgProp with From=3 into a leader whose configuration had just removed node 3 was accepted with no error and appended one entry (focused probe, native feedback only, no retained receipt). Counterevidence and boundaries: (a) the caller-authorization reading is supported not only by the silence of the contract but by DisableProposalForwarding, which exists so an operator can stop followers forwarding at all, treating forwarding as normal member behaviour; (b) RawNode users bypass the facade and can step any MsgProp, which is consistent with authorization being theirs; (c) the one caller-facing consequence I keep, without calling it a library defect, is that an application which infers membership from Propose failing will be misled after the next leader change, because the channel is silently re-enabled - that is a documentation-and-usage caveat, and the code comment already flags it; (d) the probe did not exercise the facade goroutine, so the facade half is a source reading, which is enough given the contract question is what mattered.
